newsitem.title: USA: Blacks convicted in Crown Heights murder in U.S..
newsitem.headline: Blacks convicted in Crown Heights murder in U.S..

text.p: A federal jury on Monday found two black men guilty in the fatal stabbing of a Hasidic Jew in a widely watched case stemming from 1991 racial violence in the Crown Heights section of Brooklyn.

At issue was whether the defendants were part of a racist vigilante mob that killed Yankel Rosenbaum or were scapegoats for the Jewish student's murder during four nights of rioting. The violence was one of the most serious outbreaks of unrest in New York City in many years.
The federal case charged Lemrick Nelson, 21, who was acquitted earlier of the murder in state court, with violating Rosenbaum's civil rights.
Many Hasidic Jews and elected officials demanded a federal investigation after the acquittal by the state court jury. That inquiry led to this trial.
A co-defendant, 43-year-old Charles Price, was charged with aiding and abetting the civil rights violation by inciting the crowd to seek revenge on Jews.
Both men were found guilty on Monday by a jury after four days of deliberations.
Nelson buried his head in his hands and cried when he heard the guilty verdict.
Both men face the possiblity of life in prison, although such sentences are unlikely due to circumstances and legal technicalities in the case.
Rosenbaum's brother Norman, who fought for the federal trial to take place, said: "This is one small step for justice and one giant leap for the justice system."

However, he added, "There's still the rest of the mob out there, still on the street, equally responsible for my brother's murder. Each and every person responsible for my brother's murder will be brought to justice."

The murder of Rosenbaum was sparked by a car accident in which a Hasidic driver killed a 7-year-old black boy. The incident occurred in Crown Heights, a frequent site of friction between blacks and Hasidic Jews.
At the scene of the accident, a Jewish ambulance service was the first to arrive and removed the driver who was already the subject of abuse by the quickly formed crowd.
Rosenbaum, an Australian doctoral student, was stabbed to death during the violence that followed.
The jury, which included two Jews and three blacks, came back with its verdict after watching a videotape of the scene made by a bystander.
A person who appears to be Nelson is seen briefly in the crowd on the videotape. The jury asked for that segment to be replayed several times.

Defence lawyers argued that Nelson and Price did not commit the crimes. "Lemrick Nelson was made the sacrificial lamb. The police framed him, set him up," said his lawyer Christine Yaris, during closing arguments.

The most controversial evidence was a pair of faded, baggy blue jeans Nelson was allegedly wearing when he was arrested. Yaris asked Nelson to try on the pants in court, where they fell down around his knees.
"If they don't fit now, in this courtroom they didn't fit then," Yaris said and reminded jurors that Nelson was taller and heavier now than he was five and a half years ago.

Defence lawyers also argued that other inconsistencies and conflicting testimony, including alleged admissions Nelson made to the police, his former roommate and a former girlfriend proved that Nelson was set-up.

Assistant U.S. Attorney Valerie Caproni argued that there was a common thread in the testimony that proved Nelson was responsible for Rosenbaum's death, especially statements from his ex-girlfriend Travionne Shaw.
"Travionne Shaw's testimony fits like a glove," Caproni said. "Lemrick Nelson told her a story that only one other person in the world knew and Yankel Rosenbaum took it to his grave."
